title: The History of Street Fighter | From the 1987 Arcade to Street Fighter 6
description: How Street Fighter grew from a 1987 Capcom arcade game into a fighting game legend: Street Fighter II, the famous Evo Moment 37, Street Fighter IV and V, and Street Fighter 6 in 2023.

sections.heading: The world warriors
sections.script: Hadouken. Those eight letters have been shouted in arcades, living rooms and school playgrounds for decades. Street Fighter is one of the most famous fighting game series ever made, created by Capcom, and it has shaped almost everything we know about one on one fighting games. It began in the arcades in nineteen eighty seven, exploded with Street Fighter Two in nineteen ninety one, and today it is still going strong with Street Fighter Six. In this video we walk through the whole story: the first game, the golden age, the famous tournament moment that people still talk about, and the modern comeback. Whether you grew up putting coins in an arcade machine or you started on a console last year, get ready, because round one starts right now.

sections.heading: Nineteen eighty seven: the first Street Fighter
sections.script: The first Street Fighter was released as an arcade game in nineteen eighty seven. It was designed by Takashi Nishiyama and Hiroshi Matsumoto at Capcom. The idea was a worldwide martial arts tournament. Player one controlled Ryu, a martial artist, and a second player could jump in as his friendly American rival, Ken Masters. You could perform punches and kicks, and three special moves became legends: the Hadouken fireball, the Shoryuken uppercut and the spinning Tatsumaki Senpukyaku kick. The opponents in that first game were not especially memorable, and the controls were famously tricky, but the foundations were there. Ryu and Ken, and the special moves performed with joystick motions, would become the heart of the whole series.

sections.heading: Between two games
sections.script: After the first game, two of its key creators, Takashi Nishiyama and Hiroshi Matsumoto, left Capcom for the rival company SNK. There they went on to help create the Fatal Fury and Art of Fighting series, which became hits in their own right. Meanwhile Capcom did not rush to make a sequel to Street Fighter. Instead, the company focused on a scrolling beat em up called Final Fight, which was first presented as if it might be the Street Fighter sequel. In the end it became its own series. Some of the people who worked on Final Fight would soon take over the fighting game idea, and that team was about to change video game history. The wait for a true sequel was long, but it would be worth it.

sections.heading: Nineteen ninety one: Street Fighter Two
sections.script: In nineteen ninety one Capcom released Street Fighter Two: The World Warrior. It ran on Capcom's CP System arcade hardware and was designed by Akira Nishitani and Akira Yasuda, who had also worked on Final Fight. This time players could choose from a roster of different fighters, each with their own style, their own special moves and their own personality. You could pick Ryu or Ken, but also Chun Li, Guile, Blanka, Zangief, Dhalsim and E Honda. After beating the other fighters, you faced four powerful bosses. Players could also challenge a friend at any moment, and that two player rivalry is what made arcades come alive. Capcom itself calls Street Fighter Two a global smash hit with an innovative battle system, and it turned the series into a worldwide phenomenon.

sections.heading: The Street Fighter Two family
sections.script: The success of Street Fighter Two led to a whole family of upgrades. Street Fighter Two Champion Edition made the four boss characters playable. Hyper Fighting increased the speed, partly as an answer to unofficial bootleg versions of the game. Then came Super Street Fighter Two, which added new challengers, and Super Street Fighter Two Turbo, which brought the super combo system. There is also a famous naming quirk. In the Japanese version, three of the boss characters had different names from the overseas version. The names of the final boss, the claw wielding fighter and the boxer were rotated, which is why fans still explain that the Japanese Vega is the overseas M. Bison. Even this little mix up became part of Street Fighter legend.

sections.heading: Alpha, Three and the nineties
sections.script: Through the rest of the nineteen nineties, Capcom kept the series moving. The Street Fighter Alpha games arrived with a brighter, more animated style, and filled in story between the first two games. Then in nineteen ninety seven came Street Fighter Three: New Generation. It kept only Ryu and Ken from the old roster, introduced a brand new cast, and added a defensive technique called the parry. A well timed parry could block an attack without taking damage, and it rewarded players who studied their opponent. The series later received Second Impact and Third Strike. Third Strike became especially loved by competitive players, and that is the game where one of the most famous moments in all of gaming would happen.

sections.heading: Evo Moment Thirty Seven
sections.script: The date is August first, two thousand four. At the Evolution Championship Series, known as Evo, in Pomona, California, Daigo Umehara plays Justin Wong in Street Fighter Three: Third Strike. Daigo, playing Ken, is on the edge of defeat, while Justin Wong, playing Chun Li, unleashes a super attack to finish him. What happens next is parry after parry. Daigo blocks the attack hit after hit, counters in the air and goes on to win. The crowd goes wild. A video of the match, uploaded under the name Evo Moment Thirty Seven, spread across the internet and is still widely described as one of the most iconic moments in competitive gaming history. Ten years later the two met again and Daigo repeated the feat in an exhibition match.

sections.heading: Street Fighter Four returns
sections.script: After Third Strike, the series went quiet for a long time. Street Fighter Four was the first new main game since Street Fighter Three in nineteen ninety seven. It reached Japanese arcades in July two thousand eight, and the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 versions followed in February two thousand nine. The game used three dimensional graphics for characters and stages, but it still played like the classic two dimensional Street Fighter, so fans called it two and a half D. It brought back classic fighters from Street Fighter Two, plus new fighters, and it added online play, so many longtime fans returned. Updates such as Super and Ultra Street Fighter Four kept the community busy for years.

sections.heading: Street Fighter Five
sections.script: Street Fighter Five arrived on February sixteenth, two thousand sixteen. It was available on the PlayStation 4 and on PC, with players able to compete across both platforms, and it was not released on Xbox consoles. It launched with a roster of sixteen characters, with more fighters added through updates in the following years. Over time Capcom released big updates such as Arcade Edition and Champion Edition, and the roster grew to a very large cast. Street Fighter Five also kept the esports scene alive, with tournaments around the world where champions battled for glory. It was a bigger, longer chapter than many players first expected, and it set the stage for the next big step in the series.

sections.heading: Street Fighter Six
sections.script: Street Fighter Six launched on June second, two thousand twenty three, on PlayStation 5, PlayStation 4, Xbox Series consoles and PC. It runs on Capcom's own RE Engine and offers three big game modes: Fighting Ground for classic matches, World Tour, a single player adventure with a customizable character, and Battle Hub, a social space for players. Capcom announced that it sold over one million copies within days of launch, and at that moment said the whole Street Fighter series had passed fifty million units in total sales. By June two thousand twenty six, Street Fighter Six itself had passed seven million units worldwide, according to Capcom's latest announcement. After more than thirty five years, the series is still growing.

sections.heading: Your main
sections.script: That is the story of Street Fighter, from a nineteen eighty seven arcade game to a series that has lasted for decades and still draws huge crowds today. Now we want to hear from you. Which Street Fighter game is your favorite: the original Street Fighter Two, Third Strike, Street Fighter Four, Five or Six? And who is your main fighter: Ryu, Ken, Chun Li, Guile or someone else? Tell us in the comments below. If you enjoyed this history lesson, please subscribe to the channel for more gaming history, news and guides, and we will see you in the next video.
